files.Title: Playcraft.Core.CalloutPlacement
files.Summary: Where the bubbles go: each close to its own part, in open paper (off every stroke of line work, every other bubble, the north arrow and the deck height boxes), its leader short and ending on the part's line work. Every candidate spot round each target point is scored by its leader's length plus what the leader crosses: other parts' line work, its own part's, deck boxes, and (heaviest) other leaders. The most constrained bubble is placed first; then each bubble in turn is lifted and placed again against all the others until nothing improves. A bubble that still has no spot takes the nearest clear of the other bubbles and the boxes anywhere on the plan, over line work if it must (it is filled white, so its number still reads).

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.CatalogSearch
files.Summary:
The catalog search: how a designer's typing turns into a ranked list.

Three things the plain substring filter it replaces could not do. It ranks, so typing "deck" puts the square deck above the hundred parts whose DESCRIPTION happens to say "deck". It ignores punctuation in part numbers, so S-1101-R5, s1101r5 and 1101 all find the same deck. And when a query matches nothing at all it retries with a bounded edit distance, so one fat-fingered letter returns the part instead of an empty list — but only then, and it says so, because a fuzzy match that quietly displaces exact ones is worse than no match.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.CatalogSearchResult
files.Summary: What a search found: the entries in relevance order, plus the near-miss term when nothing matched exactly and the search fell back to spelling tolerance. is non-null only in that case, so the palette can say the results are approximate instead of pretending.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.CatalogSort
files.Summary: Sorting for the catalog palette. One rule is worth stating out loud: a part with no price sorts LAST whichever direction the price column is pointing. Ascending, an unpriced part is not "cheapest"; descending, it is not "most expensive". Missing data is missing data, and letting it win either end of the list is how a designer picks a part believing something the catalog never said.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.KcdLayerAudit
files.Summary:
Layer-vs-geometry disagreement report for an imported design file (ADR §4.4c's deferred import half). The legacy app cannot run this check on itself — a 2D canvas has no answer to "what stands on what" — so the designer's hand-typed tiers go unexamined until the texted top view splits into unreadable pages. The suite derives the storeys and can say where the file's own numbers contradict them.

This is a REPORT, never a correction: adoption of the file's numbering — including a privately inverted one — is the §4.4c rule, so the audit compares the PARTITION, not the labels. A walkable band wholly labeled 3 is consistent; a band split between two labels is not. On the reference corpus (11 files, 113 decks) the checks flag nothing, so a finding on a real file is signal, not noise.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.KcdLayers
files.Summary:
Layer (storey/tier) assignment for components added to a design file (ADR §4.4c). The file's <Layer> integer is the legacy designer's hand-typed storey index — it filters the build in the Layer Manager and splits the texted top-view PDF into one page per tier. The legacy app cannot compute it (a 2D canvas has no answer to "what stands on what"), so designers maintain it by hand; the suite can, so additions derive their tier and an existing component's Layer is treated as designer evidence that is never rewritten and never "corrected".

Corpus-measured before writing (reference kcds, 9 multi-layer tabs, 128 deck placements): designer layers are clean non-interleaving height bands 9/9; the traversal tier below reproduces 102/128 hand assignments, and the misses are one file with privately inverted numbering (adoption keeps it) and tiers reached only by climbing links (adoption inherits them from the file's own bands). Height ALONE cannot draw the band line — the corpus holds a between-band gap equal to the largest within-band step (both 24") — which is why adjacency and footprint coincidence participate.

The legacy app cannot be run here, so the envelope is deliberately a compatibility superset of the available evidence (the corpus and the legacy loader; citations in the source comments): the loader's hard requirements, the newest corpus writer's shape, both underlay forms, a complete production color scheme (an incomplete one opens but blocks saving in the legacy app), and the legacy writer's own empty-thumbnail fallback. Its hardware counts start at zero and are not left there: the order system prices them exactly as written, so the writer fills in each tab's real counts once its parts are in.

files.Summary: Post-identity assignment for components added to a design file. A slot's PostID is the file's identity for a physical post: slots on different components sharing an id are one post, and the design's post count is the number of distinct ids. New slots therefore inherit the id of any post they land on and mint fresh ids otherwise.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.KcdPostReconciliation
files.Summary: A design tab's post ids resolved against its own components. A slot's PostID has two meanings the legacy format never separates: most name a placed component (an insertable, surface-mount or Revolution post — the component IS the post), and the rest are abstract identities for posts that exist only as shared bookkeeping between deck corners. Counting the two as one number is what made real designs look wrong: a file whose every post is a placed component "declares" as many ids as it has post components, and comparing that against a geometric slot merge measures nothing. This record separates them so each part can be judged by the rule that actually applies to it.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.McpUndoJournal
files.Summary: A drawing's undo list as far as the assistant can account for it, newest last. Every command leaves one step on AutoCAD's undo list, even one that changed nothing. An assistant call runs inside PBMCPRUN or PBMCP, so each of those commands is a step the journal knows: a change, or empty (reads, refusals). Anything else, a designer's command or a change made outside any command, is a step the journal cannot see past, so it forgets everything below it. Undo is then AutoCAD's own UNDO, run inside the assistant's command, for the empty steps on top plus the newest change: it takes back everything that change did, posts and fillers included, because AutoCAD recorded all of it.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.NameFinishes
files.Summary:
The finish a mesh or layer name says when the colour data has nothing for it. About one mesh in six in the library's models matches no material prefix (stainless hardware, galvanised chain, Lexan windows, black handles and caps), but the people who modelled them wrote the finish into the name. Rules, first match wins:

  1. Materials with their own finish: Lexan is clear and see-through (in the colour its name says, if any), a mirror is a mirror, galvanised chain and stainless, chrome or aluminium hardware are bare metal, rubber is black, a tyre is a fixed dark finish, a swing anti-wrap sleeve is black.
  2. "Metallic" with no colour is bare metal.
  3. A colour word in the name is that colour: powder coat when the name says powder coat or metal, plastic otherwise.
Names that say nothing about a finish (dummies, cameras, lights, posts and panels that should follow the scheme but have no colour entry) stay unresolved: guessing a fixed colour for them would hide the missing entry. Revolution posts and plugs are not here: they follow the post colour ().

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.PostReconciler
files.Summary:
Diffs the drawing's posts against a plan. Matching is by position within the merge tolerance, so a kept post keeps its handle: this retires erase-and-remint for posts (ADR §4.2's deferred row, narrowed to fillers). Rules per matched post, the re-size policy among them:

  • held (nested, xref, locked layer): never written; reported when it disagrees;
  • a designer's cut post (): never touched, reported when it disagrees. The legacy tool re-sizes cut posts because its guard reads the wrong field; ours protects them (decision #11);
  • Post Insertable: re-sized upward only, reported when the plan wants it shorter, kept when its last owner goes (PC2D:3322-3331; DTF:15987). The new block keeps the P- file name while its part number is the standard S-10xx-…-xxft, as the legacy tool files them;
  • any other designer post (not the suite's own, not insertable): never re-sized, reported when it disagrees. It is the design's own component and quotes as one;
  • the suite's own posts, whatever their encoding: re-sized to the plan, both ways, except that a post one of whose owners has no post facts (the rule skipped it) is only lengthened, never shortened: the plan is then a floor, and the unread owner may need more.
An unmatched plugin post is deleted, unless it records an owner whose posts could not be read (); other unmatched posts are kept and reported (the suite never erases a designer's part). A planned post with no drawing post is added, or reported when refused. Under every re-size and removal is reported instead.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SectionKind
files.Summary: What KIND of thing a quote section is, which is what orders a quote. The kind is carried alongside the name rather than sniffed out of it: a section named "Site Amenities" could be a designer's group or a family roll-up, and only the code that resolved it knows which.

files.Summary: Item 34 C: select by kind. PBSELECT (and the palette's Select list) leaves a native AutoCAD selection of one kind of part, so MOVE, ERASE and Properties work on it. This holds the kinds, their words, the one-line report and the two rules that need more than a family: the play event (the catalog's own EventType, the field the legacy tool's ADA counts read) and "connected" (the structure graph the plugin already builds: mate points, posts, walls, roofs).

files.Summary: What one structure (a designer's named group, or the drawing default every loose part and every new structure reads) declares about itself: its age range, rail system, mounting, post material, and whether it takes IPEMA-certified parts only. Every field may be unset (null, or false for the IPEMA flag); each rule that reads a field says what it does when it is unset. The product type is not here: it is derived from the structure's parts (), and applies what it forces.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.StructureSpec

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.StructureZone
files.Summary: One structure's use zone: the union of its parts' zones of every kind.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SubItemExploder
files.Summary: Explodes a tallied BOM into its sub-components by walking the parent → child links in PartsSubItems. Pure: the caller supplies the row lookup, so the walk is unit-testable without a database and the Cad layer's only job is running one query per level.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SubItemExplosion
files.Summary: An explosion pass: the sub-component lines plus what the pass could not trust. The notes exist because this data is hand-maintained — a silently dropped cycle or an unreadable quantity would turn into a short purchase list, so callers report them rather than presenting a clean total.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SubItemLine
files.Summary: One exploded sub-component: a part the drawing needs because a top-level component contains it.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SubItemRow
files.Summary: One PartsSubItems row as the explosion sees it. Every numeric column in that table is nvarchar, so the values arrive as raw text and are parsed here rather than at the database boundary — a price of "" or a quantity of "AR" is data the BOM has to survive, not an exception.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SurfaceFinish

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SwingResult

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.SystemRules
files.Summary: What a structure's rail system accepts: which parts and families it shows, and which posts it builds. Pure; the catalog filter, the audit and the post planner all ask here.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.TitleBlock
files.Summary: The sheet frame and title block for each paper size, and the values its fields print.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.TooWideCell
files.Summary: A cell too wide for its column: reported, never squeezed.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.TooWideField
files.Summary: A field whose value is wider than the room the title block gives it.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.Transform2
files.Summary: The XY part of a placed block's transform (rotation / mirror / scale plus translation) — the bridge from mate-table coordinates, which are local to a part's insertion point, to world coordinates. Kept in Core so every consumer of mate positions (the click path, the F-032 jig, the F-033 osnap overrule) runs the identical transform math and can never disagree about where a mate point is.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.UnitPrices
files.Summary: Unit prices for one part: retail and (when known) discounted.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.UnmatchedFootingMarker
files.Summary: A footing marker in a part's drawing with no library point: reported, never added.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.UnmatchedSidecarPoint
files.Summary: A sidecar point no drawing marker sat on.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultAttachmentPoint
files.Summary: A component attachment point: where a dependent part attaches.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultComponent
files.Summary: A component parsed from a component-library 2D SVG. All coordinates are local to the component's insertion point with Y up (SVG is Y-down), in inches.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultDescription
files.Summary: What a library turned out to contain, for reporting before trusting it.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultFiles
files.Summary: The one way into the component library's files (Global Invariant 10: the library is read-only in every respect). Every path the suite builds into the library comes from here, and every read here opens the file for reading only, sharing it with anyone else. Nothing here, or anywhere else in src, opens a library file for writing; a source-discipline test holds that line.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultFootingPoint
files.Summary: A component footing point: where it meets the ground and the footing it takes.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultInventory
files.Summary: Inspects a library before trusting it: what is there, where, and which data files are missing, in plain sentences for PBSETUP, PBVAULT and the load-time banner. Reads through , so it assumes no layout at all and shares the session's one walk.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultMatePoint
files.Summary: A component mate point: where another component attaches and which way it faces.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultPolyline
files.Summary: One connected polyline run: vertices with AutoCAD-style bulges (bulge[i] curves the segment from vertex i to i+1; tan(sweep/4)).

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultSvgParser
files.Summary: Minimal parser for the component library's machine-generated SVGs. They use a constrained vocabulary: a JSON metadata block (insertion point, post slots, mate points) and path elements using only absolute M/L/A/Z commands. Anything outside that vocabulary throws — callers fall back to placeholder geometry rather than render a wrong shape.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.VaultXamlParser
files.Summary: Parser for the component library's native 2D geometry files — the legacy designer's own Component2D XAML ("{folder}.xaml"), the format the recovered library actually ships. It carries the same attachment metadata a design file's placed component does: the insertion point, the post slots (with their height offsets, and the Revolution slots some parts add), the mate points (with their length class and mate-type), the footing points, the attachment points, and the file's own part number, revision and design height — everything the library sidecar migrates from it. Produces the same contract as , so every downstream consumer (block build, filler pairing, mate snap) is source-agnostic.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.WhatFits
files.Summary: Item 34 A, "what fits here": the parts that fit one of the selected part's FREE mate points, by the same mate rules, family check and occupancy the magnet uses (, ), and rated for its height at the structure's ages by the envelope PBFIT and the placement note use ().

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.WhatFitsResult
files.Summary: What "what fits here" found for one selected part: its free points, the parts that fit one of them, and the parts that mate with it but are left out, with the reason. A part that cannot mate with it at all is neither: it is simply not listed.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.Xaml3DAssets
files.Summary: Filename preference for the library's exported 3D models ("{folder}-3D.xaml"). Pure string work so the tolerance rules are testable: the vault is hand-maintained and its known misnamings — a "-3D2" suffix, a "-3D_NEW" variant, two parts' files sharing one misfiled folder — must resolve to the right model instead of silently dropping the part.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.Xaml3DMeshes
files.Summary: Minimal reader for the component library's exported 3D XAML models. It extracts collar mesh bounding boxes — the input to — by scanning MeshGeometry3D resources whose key starts with Collar_ (case-insensitive across the library's old COLLAR_ and current Collar_ conventions; CollarHW_ is hardware, not a collar, and never matches because of the underscore), and the R3.5 collars keyed KCR35_. Pure text parsing — no WPF — so it runs and tests headlessly.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.XamlGlb
files.Summary: A part's .glb made from its 3D XAML model, ready to write.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.XamlMeshRead
files.Summary: What reading one part's 3D XAML model gave.

files.Title: Playcraft.Core.XamlPartMesh
files.Summary: The fallback 3D model of a part that has no 3D drawing: its older -3D.xaml model (WPF 3D markup), read as plain XML, turned into the drawing frame and grouped by material layer, so it can be written as a .glb exactly like a drawing-built one ().
